passage:
Monday, 9 p.m. Seema stared at the same configuration error for an hour. She had tried three fixes from the internet and each made it worse. She closed the laptop and opened it again.
Tuesday morning. She wrote in the team chat: "Getting 'port already in use' on startup. Here is the exact message. I checked the running processes and restarted the machine. Still happens. Any idea?" She attached a screenshot. Ten minutes later Madhuri, the senior, wrote a two-line reply about a leftover process and the command to find it.
Friday. Seema fixed a junior's similar error in five minutes. "I read your message on Tuesday," she said to Madhuri. "It was a good question." Madhuri smiled. "It was easy to answer."

qa.q: What error did Seema get on Tuesday morning?
qa.a: Seema got 'port already in use' on startup.

qa.q: What is Seema feeling on Monday night after an hour on the error?
qa.a: Seema is frustrated and stuck, closing the laptop and opening it again, with fixes that made things worse.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Seema use if Madhuri were unavailable, and why?
qa.a: Seema could search the exact error text in the tool's issue list or forum, because an exact message often matches someone else's solved problem.

qa.q: How might Madhuri see Seema's message?
qa.a: Madhuri sees a clear question with the exact message and steps tried, so it is easy to answer in a couple of lines, which is why Madhuri smiles about it.

grounding: Shows asking a senior for help at a stuck point with a clear, specific question and getting a quick answer.

subtype: Approach: asking an expert or senior at a stuck point [Action]
passage:
Tanvir, you've been staring at that red text for how long? An hour? Let me, Arohi, tell you what happened to me in my first month here.
I was twenty-one, setting up the build for a small mobile project, and one configuration error would not go away. I reinstalled things, changed versions, restarted. Fifty-five minutes gone. I was proud and did not want to look stupid.
Then I remembered what a senior at college had drilled into us: after an hour, ask, but ask properly. So I wrote in the team channel: the full error text, what I was trying to do, and the three things I had already tried.
Ten minutes later a senior developer replied. One line was pointing to an old folder path. Ten minutes, after my hour.
So open the channel now, and write it the way I did.

qa.q: What three things did Arohi put into the question?
qa.a: The full error text, what was being tried, and the three things already tried.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling during those fifty-five minutes, and why not ask sooner?
qa.a: Arohi felt proud and was afraid of looking stupid, so asking felt harder than trying one more fix.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made the difference?
qa.a: Remembering the college senior's rule, after an hour ask properly, turned a stuck hour into a ten-minute fix.

qa.q: How might the senior developer in the story have seen Arohi's question?
qa.a: It was easy to answer because the full error and the steps tried were there, so the senior could spot the old folder path quickly.

grounding: Shows a senior colleague recalling an hour stuck on a configuration error, then posting a clear question with the error and steps tried and getting an answer in ten minutes.

subtype: Approach: asking an expert or senior at a stuck point [Action]
passage:
The hackathon hall was loud, submissions closed at 6 p.m., and Pallavi had been fighting one configuration error since 3:40 in a tool she had installed that morning. At 4:45 she stopped.
She copied the exact error text, then wrote three lines under it: what she was trying to run, the two fixes she had tried, and the version numbers. She posted it on the event's help board and tagged the mentors.
Parveen, a final-year student volunteering as a mentor, saw it between two other questions. Because everything was there, one reading was enough. 'Your settings file is in the wrong folder,' Parveen typed at 4:55. Pallavi moved it. The build turned green.
At 5:58, with the hall still roaring and her battery at nine percent, her team submitted.

qa.q: How was Pallavi feeling at 4:45, and what did she do with that feeling?
qa.a: She was likely stressed by the 6 p.m. deadline and the hour lost, but calm enough to stop and write a careful question.

qa.q: Which approach would have suited Pallavi better at 3:40?
qa.a: With the deadline so close, a shorter limit before posting the same clear question would have saved even more time.

qa.q: How did the post look to Parveen, who was juggling other questions?
qa.a: It was a relief for Parveen, because the error text, steps and versions were all there, so one reading was enough.

grounding: Shows a student at a hackathon, blocked for an hour on a configuration error, posting a clear question with the error text and steps tried and getting an answer in ten minutes.
